title: Pairs
directAnswer: Count the pairs of elements whose difference is exactly k. Sort the array, then for each value x do a binary search for x + k; every hit is one valid pair. Sorting makes the lookup O(log n), so the whole thing is O(n log n). Because the values are distinct, each pair is found exactly once (search forward for the larger partner). A sorted two-pointer sweep is the equivalent O(n)-after-sort alternative.

remember.pattern: Sort, then binary-search for x + k (the larger partner)
rules: Search for `x + k`, the **larger** partner — each pair `(x, x+k)` is then discovered exactly once, from its smaller side.
The array values are **distinct**, so a found target is one unique pair (no multiplicity bookkeeping).
Sort **first**: binary search and two-pointer both require sorted input.
Difference is **exact** (`= k`), not `≤ k` — use an exact-match search, not a boundary/upper-bound count.
Equivalent O(n) sweep: two pointers `i`, `j`; advance `j` while `arr[j] − arr[i] < k`, count on equality, advance `i` otherwise.
whenToUse: Count pairs satisfying an exact additive relation in a set of distinct values
You can sort, and each query becomes 'does value v exist?'
A 'difference equals k' / 'sum equals target' count over a static array
antiSignals: Difference ≤ k (a range, not exact) → two-pointer window counting instead of exact search
Duplicates allowed and pairs counted with multiplicity → use a frequency map, not a set
Values fit in a small range → a boolean presence array beats sorting
remember.takeaway: Sorting turns 'find a partner with an exact difference' into an O(log n) existence query. Always search for the larger partner (x + k) so each pair is counted once — or sweep two pointers for the same result without per-element search overhead.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you move from the O(n²) all-pairs scan to a sorted structure that answers 'does x + k exist?' in O(log n) — and whether you avoid double counting by searching only for the larger partner.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Searching for both x + k and x − k (double counting each pair), comparing |a − b| in a nested loop and timing out, or using an exact search where the values aren't sorted.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that searching only for x + k counts each pair once by construction, then offer the two-pointer sweep as an even cleaner O(n)-after-sort variant and mention a hash set as an O(n) average alternative.

problemStatement:
Given an array of `n` **distinct** integers and a target value `k`, count the number of unordered pairs of elements whose **difference is exactly k**.

That is, count the pairs `(a, b)` with `a − b = k` (equivalently `|a − b| = k`), where `a` and `b` are two different elements of the array.
understanding: Every valid pair consists of a smaller value x and a larger value x + k. If we sort the array, the question 'is there a partner for x?' becomes 'does x + k appear in the array?', answerable by binary search in O(log n). Counting from the smaller side (searching for x + k) guarantees each pair is counted exactly once. Distinct values mean a found target contributes exactly one pair.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the difference exact, or at most k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Exact: a − b = k. That calls for an exact-match search, not a count of everything within a range.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the elements distinct?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. So a successful search for x + k means exactly one pair — no need to multiply by frequencies.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are pairs ordered or unordered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Unordered: (a, b) and (b, a) are the same pair. Searching only for the larger partner x + k counts each once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could x + k overflow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: arr[i] < 2³¹ and k < 10⁹, so x + k can exceed the signed 32-bit range. Use a 64-bit type (long) for the search key, or be careful in languages with fixed-width ints.

approaches.name: Brute Force — All Pairs
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to fix the definition, then note the O(n²) cost at n = 10⁵.
hints: What's the most direct way to test whether two elements differ by exactly k?
Compare every unordered pair (i, j) with i < j and check if their difference equals k.
Increment a counter on each match; no early exit since we want the total count.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two nested loops over all i < j → n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 comparisons, O(n²).
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading: a valid pair is two elements whose difference is k. Enumerate every unordered pair and count the matches.

**Why i < j.** Starting the inner loop at i + 1 visits each unordered pair once and never compares an element with itself, so we don't double count or self-match.

**Why absolute difference.** Using `Math.abs(arr[i] − arr[j]) == k` handles either ordering of the two values within the pair.

**Why we don't ship it.** With n up to 10⁵, n²/2 ≈ 5×10⁹ comparisons is too slow. Sorting plus binary search (or a single hash-set pass) brings it down dramatically.
approaches.insight: The inner loop re-asks 'is there a partner for arr[i]?' by scanning everything. That repeated existence question is exactly what a sorted array + binary search (or a hash set) answers in sub-linear / constant time.

approaches.name: Sort + Binary Search (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want: sort once, then an O(log n) existence query per element for the larger partner.
hints: If the array were sorted, how could you check whether a specific partner value exists without scanning?
For each x, its larger partner is x + k. Binary search the sorted array for that exact value.
Count one for each successful search. Searching only for x + k (the larger side) counts each pair exactly once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). Then n binary searches at O(log n) each → O(n log n). No extra space beyond the sort (O(1) auxiliary).
approaches.explanation:
Sort the array. Now every value x has a unique potential partner `x + k` (the larger element of the pair). Binary search the sorted array for `x + k`; each hit is one valid pair.

**Why search for the larger partner only.** A pair `(x, x + k)` could be discovered from either side — from x looking up for `x + k`, or from `x + k` looking down for x. To count it exactly once, we fix a direction: every value searches *upward* for `x + k`. The smaller member of each pair finds the larger; the larger member searches for an even larger value that completes a *different* pair (or none). No pair is counted twice and none is missed.

**Why distinct values simplify it.** Since all elements are distinct, a successful search means exactly one partner exists — the count increments by one, with no frequency multiplication.

**Why exact match, not a boundary search.** The difference must equal k exactly, so we need plain 'does `x + k` exist?' — an equality binary search. (If the problem asked for difference ≤ k, we'd switch to counting a range via two pointers.)

**Overflow note.** `x + k` can exceed 2³¹ since x < 2³¹ and k < 10⁹. Compute the key in a 64-bit type (long) before searching to avoid wraparound.

**Two-pointer equivalent.** On the sorted array, keep two indices i ≤ j: advance j while `arr[j] − arr[i] < k`; if it equals k, count and advance both; if it exceeds k, advance i. That's O(n) after the sort and avoids the per-element log factor — mention it as the streamlined alternative.
approaches.insight: Sorting converts a quadratic 'find a partner for everyone' into a logarithmic existence test, and fixing the search direction (always look up for x + k) is the clean trick that prevents double counting without any extra bookkeeping. The same sort-then-search shape solves 'two sum on a sorted array' and 'count pairs with a given difference/sum'.

pitfalls: Also searching for x − k — counts every pair twice.
Forgetting to widen x + k to long — overflow for large values.
Using an exact search on an unsorted array — sort first.

commonMistakes: Searching for both x + k and x − k, double counting every pair.
Comparing all pairs in a nested loop and timing out on 10⁵ elements.
Letting x + k overflow a 32-bit int before the search.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Double counting by searching both directions
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you look for both x + k and x − k, each pair is discovered from both members and counted twice. Fix one direction.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if found(arr, x + k): count += 1
if found(arr, x - k): count += 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good: if found(arr, x + k): count += 1   # larger partner only

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Exact search on unsorted data
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Binary search assumes sorted order; running it on the raw input returns wrong (or random) results.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// no sort
for (int x : arr) if (binarySearch(arr, (long) x + k)) count++;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
java.util.Arrays.sort(arr);
for (int x : arr) if (binarySearch(arr, (long) x + k)) count++;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow on the partner value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: x < 2³¹ and k < 10⁹, so x + k can exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE and wrap negative, breaking the search.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: binarySearch(arr, x + k);          // int + int can overflow
